name: Tailoring (any clothes)
lead: Tailoring, in the sense used in style and grooming discussions, is the practice of having a tailor alter ready-made clothing so that it follows the wearer's measurements, for example by hemming trousers, taking in a shirt or shortening sleeves. A tailor is a person who makes or alters clothing, particularly men's clothing, and the English term is dated by the Oxford English Dictionary to the thirteenth century.[1] A more extensive service, often called bespoke or made-to-measure, constructs a garment from scratch using custom patterns and several fittings, whereas alterations are smaller adjustments to existing garments that are generally quicker and cheaper.[2]

In appearance advice, fit is commonly described as mattering more than brand or price, and altering off-the-rack clothes is presented as a low-cost way to change how a physique and outfit read. This idea circulates mainly in fashion practice and style communities rather than in the scientific literature. No clinical trials or other controlled studies of garment alteration and perceived attractiveness were located in the sources reviewed for this article.

The craft itself has a long documented history, including medieval guilds, apprenticeship systems, regional house styles and the later growth of ready-to-wear clothing that made alteration a separate everyday service.[1][2]
infobox: Unregulated trade (no clearance or approval process)

paras: Alterations modify a finished garment: trouser hems and waistbands, shirt sides and sleeve lengths, and jacket sleeves are common examples. Because the work removes or repositions fabric within the garment's existing seam allowances, how much can be changed depends on how the piece was originally cut.[2]

Bespoke tailoring is a separate and more involved process in which patterns are drafted for the individual client. Wikipedia notes that even with modern machinery a large share of the stitching in a custom-tailored suit is still done by hand, and that some cutters work by eye with chalk rather than from numerical drafts.[1] Made-to-measure sits between the two, adjusting an existing pattern to a client's measurements.[2]

Tailoring traditions are described in terms of regional house styles. The British cut is characterised in descriptions of it by a defined waist and structured shoulders built with heavier canvassing and fabrics, and is associated with houses such as Henry Poole and H. Huntsman and Sons. The Italian cut is described as lighter and softer, with fabrics of lower weight and more natural shoulders, and Cesare Attolini is credited with the lighter Neapolitan construction. The American cut is described as a blend of the two, fuller in shape with a lightly padded natural shoulder, and the Ivy League look is its best-known form.[1]

Wikipedia reports evidence of tailor shops and tailoring tools such as shears and irons in ancient Greece and Rome, and a formalised profession in medieval Europe organised through guilds with masters, journeymen and apprentices. In 1244 tailors in Bologna adopted statutes governing their trade, and in England the Statute of Artificers of 1563 listed tailoring among trades entered by apprenticeship, typically of seven years.[1] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, similarly describes tailoring as emerging between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries as fashions shifted to fitted garments, and places the London tailors' fraternity in records from about 1300.[2]

Padding men's jackets with underlayers became fashionable in Europe by the fourteenth century, and by the nineteenth century garments were fitted to the wearer with a more subtle understructure.[1] The earliest surviving treatise on cutting by a tailor is attributed to Juan de Alcega of Spain in 1580, and published patterns became widely available in the late eighteenth century, after which patterns had earlier been treated as trade secrets.[1]

In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries the trade became more specialised and, in Britain, a major employer; the 1851 census counted 152,672 tailors, and cheap ready-made clothing known as slops was one factor in changing working conditions.[1] Later mechanisation of cloth and the sewing machine supported mass-produced ready-to-wear clothing, which in turn created the market for alteration of finished garments.[2]

sections.h: How it is said to work
paras: Proponents describe the mechanism as geometric: when shoulders, waist, sleeve and hem lengths line up with the wearer's body, the garment follows the body's lines rather than hanging loosely or pulling. This account comes from style practice and has not itself been tested in published experiments on alteration.

No published study located for this article has measured whether altered clothing changes ratings of attractiveness or status. General research on clothing and first impressions exists, but it was not examined as a test of alteration specifically.

The site-level rating describes the effect as immediate but temporary, since it depends on wearing the altered garment. Supporting evidence is largely anecdotal and professional: tailors, stylists and clothing writers say that well-fitted ordinary clothing can look better than poorly fitted expensive clothing. No controlled studies were found to confirm or quantify this.

There are no medical risks associated with garment alteration. Practical limits are reported by the trade: alteration is constrained by seam allowances and the original construction, and some garments cannot be reshaped satisfactorily. A poorly executed alteration can damage a piece, and the cost of alterations relative to the garment price varies.[2]

In looksmaxxing and wider men's style discussion, tailoring is typically placed among the inexpensive, low-risk steps for improving presentation, usually described as a way to make a given physique appear more proportionate without surgical or pharmacological intervention. The wiki's own summary of the topic describes it as an instant upgrade for the money spent and says fit matters more than brand.
